8358 kW Temporary Roboport Optimal:
https://factoriobin.com/post/yyvxsq


Footnotes:

[1] - As will become clear, when I say "fixed" footprint, I mean "fixed area" footprint. 
[2] - The design seen here is not the same as the blueprint. That is because the buildings that wrap around the sides have been shifted so that the tile also works standalone.
[3] - In a potential 100 by 100 setup, two roboports is enough to maintain logistic connection, but as some of you might have noticed, is not enough to have the entire array within building range, so the building stage will be somewhat annoying.
[4] - As will become clear in the results section, both the set-it-and-forget it design and the temporary roboport desing will be optimized. 
[5] - All 8316 kW options in the chart are equivalent in terms of solar panels and accumulators. As you can see, they all have the same number of both, the difference between them is a tradeoff between substations and 1 by 1 tiles or medium poles, i.e.: all 8316 kW setups have networks taking up to 46 tiles. The difference betwen them is how that is split up. The setups lower in the charts free up more spaces by lowering the substation count.
[6] - Similarly to [5], all 8358 kW setups just differ in their network. The total space available to the electrics is 33 tiles. My optimal setup has a 7 substation + up to 5 medium poles, but it could also be achieved with 6 + up to 9, or 5 + up to 14, which are two other 8358 kW blocks in the chart. The 8316 kW permanent roboport theoretical best I found and showcase later in the video is a 5 + 10. 6 + 6 could also work, but in this case it ended up being better to have 4 independent medium poles instead of a substation.
[7] - i = 1173 is the index corresponding to grid position (23, 23) so its the lower corner of the roboport. The corresponding index in the full vector is i = 8673.
[8] - To clarify what the MILP solver does for us; its the actual solving of the equations, but we need to tell it what equations have to be solved in the first place. That is why this next section of the video is dedicated to the definition of the constraints. What we want is a mathematical model of our system through a vector of variables, and then a set of equations which, if fulfilled by our x vector, guarantee a solution to the problem. Once those equations are defined, the MILP solver takes on from there. I could make a MILP solver myself, but professional and very fast solvers exist already, our time is much better dedicated to problem definition.
[9] - Counting buildings by just adding up the variables in the corresponding slice of vector x is a huge advantage of the binary formulation. Other formulations exist for packing problems, mostly building coordinate based ones. But the problem with those is that we need to know the building counts beforehand. In this problem, we don't. Or at least not initially. Although for the final optimality bridge I did end up using some coordinate based formulations for Stage A.
[10] - I mentioned this already, but I made the array be toroidal, meaning that a building placed across the border wraps around to the other side. You can see this here with accumulator x3, which uses tiles 0 and 4 too.
[11] - On account of the number of variables, matrices in this problem are very big, but fortunately relatively sparse, meaning most of their elements are 0. That makes it easier to save them in memory. 
However, most of my code does not really bother defining matrices as sparse, basically because I have the RAM required to fully construct them, and the connectivity C is very dense anyway. Finally, the definition would affect the speed of the problem building, but not the speed of the actual solving because the MILP algorithm is what takes care of that.
[12] - We could free up the root by adding another 2500 variables to identify its position through binary. That was one of the restriction relaxations I used to ultimately bridge the gap to optimality.
